influences/platonism-in-theology/name: Platonism and Middle Platonism in early theology
influences/platonism-in-theology/sourceC: Platonic and Middle Platonic teaching on a transcendent, incorporeal God, the immortal soul and the intelligible world
influences/platonism-in-theology/christi: The conceptual vocabulary of patristic theology: divine simplicity and immutability, the soul’s ascent, allegorical exegesis and the Logos as mediator
influences/platonism-in-theology/evidenc: The use of Platonic and Middle Platonic concepts by Justin, Clement, Origen, the Cappadocians and Augustine is explicit in their own writings; what is debated is how far this changed the substance of the faith rather than its idiom.
influences/platonism-in-theology/popular: Christianity is ‘Platonism for the people’ (Nietzsche): the church fathers replaced the Hebrew faith of Jesus with Greek philosophy, so that doctrines such as the immortal soul or the Trinity are really Plato in disguise.
influences/platonism-in-theology/whatHis: Historians agree that the Fathers used Platonism deliberately and openly, above all the Middle Platonism of the first and second centuries (Plutarch, Alcinous, Numenius) and Philo of Alexandria’s Jewish synthesis. They also stress what the Fathers refused: the eternity of matter, the Demiurge working on pre-existing stuff, the body as a prison, and a hierarchy of lesser gods. Creation out of nothing, the incarnation and the resurrection of the body ran directly against Platonic assumptions. Adolf von Harnack’s ‘Hellenisation of Christianity’ thesis is now widely qualified; scholars such as Pelikan and Ayres speak equally of a ‘Christianisation of Hellenism’, in which borrowed terms were bent to new ends.
influences/platonism-in-theology/summary: From the second century Christian thinkers used the dominant philosophy of the Roman world, Platonism, to explain the biblical God to educated pagans and to themselves. The borrowing of concepts and vocabulary is well documented and acknowledged by the Fathers themselves; the claim that core Christian beliefs were simply invented from Plato is not supported.
influences/platonism-in-theology/story:
By the time Christianity spread through the Greek-speaking cities, the most influential philosophy was a revived Platonism that historians call Middle Platonism (c. 80 BC–AD 220). Writers such as Plutarch, Alcinous (author of the Didaskalikos) and Numenius taught a single transcendent First God beyond all being, a secondary divine mind or Logos that ordered the world, and an immortal soul whose goal was ‘likeness to God’ (Theaetetus 176b). Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC–AD 50) had already read the Torah through these categories, interpreting Genesis allegorically and calling the Logos God’s ‘first-born’. Christian intellectuals inherited both the philosophy and Philo’s method.

Justin Martyr, who tells us he had been a Platonist before his conversion (Dialogue with Trypho 2–8), argued that Plato had glimpsed truths about God because he borrowed from Moses and because the Logos had sown ‘seeds’ of truth in all people. In Alexandria, Clement (c. 150–215) called philosophy a ‘schoolmaster’ that prepared the Greeks for Christ as the Law had prepared the Jews (Stromata 1.5). Origen (c. 185–253) built the most ambitious system: an eternal generation of the Son, a hierarchy of rational beings, the pre-existence of souls, and a threefold sense of Scripture. Some of his Platonising speculations, especially the pre-existence of souls and a universal restoration, were condemned under Justinian in 543 and at the Second Council of Constantinople in 553.

In the fourth century the Cappadocians — Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus and above all Gregory of Nyssa — used Platonic themes of ascent, participation and endless desire for God, while insisting against the Arians that the Son and Spirit are not lesser intermediaries but fully God. Here Christian thinkers rejected a central Middle Platonic idea, the subordinate ‘second god’. In the Latin West, Augustine read ‘certain books of the Platonists’ in Milan in 386 (Confessions 7.9) and credited them with freeing him from materialist ideas of God, while noting that he did not find in them that ‘the Word became flesh’.

The extent of the influence was already contested in antiquity. Tertullian asked ‘What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?’ and blamed philosophy for heresy, though he himself used Stoic ideas freely. In the nineteenth century Adolf von Harnack argued that dogma was ‘a work of the Greek spirit on the soil of the Gospel’, and many Protestant scholars contrasted Hebrew and Greek thought sharply. Since the mid-twentieth century that contrast has been softened: Hellenistic Judaism was itself shaped by Greek thought, and the creeds often used Greek terms precisely to exclude philosophical solutions (for example, homoousios against a graded hierarchy of divinity).

The outcome was a lasting partnership. The doctrines of divine simplicity and impassibility, the language of the soul’s ascent, and much of the Christian mystical tradition owe their form to Platonism. Yet the Fathers consistently subordinated it to Scripture and the rule of faith, and the distinctively Christian claims — creation from nothing, incarnation, bodily resurrection, a God who acts in history — were the points at which they parted company with the philosophers.
influences/platonism-in-theology/howItHa: Hellenistic Judaism, above all Philo of Alexandria, had already joined biblical faith to Platonic categories before the church began.
Converts trained in philosophy, such as Justin Martyr, brought their education with them and used it in apologetics addressed to emperors and the educated public.
The catechetical school of Alexandria under Clement and Origen made philosophy part of a Christian curriculum.
Debates over the Trinity forced theologians to use philosophical terms such as ousia and hypostasis with new precision, often against Platonic hierarchy.
Augustine’s synthesis transmitted a Christianised Platonism to the entire medieval West.
influences/platonism-in-theology/example: Justin Martyr’s claim that Plato borrowed from Moses (1 Apology 59–60).
Origen’s On First Principles (c. 220–230), with its pre-existent souls later condemned in 553.
Gregory of Nyssa’s Life of Moses, describing the soul’s endless ascent (epektasis).
Augustine’s account of reading the ‘books of the Platonists’ (Confessions 7.9–21) and his praise of Plato in City of God 8.
The doctrine of divine impassibility and simplicity, expressed in Platonic vocabulary but anchored in texts such as Malachi 3:6 and James 1:17.
influences/platonism-in-theology/defende: Held that Plato and the philosophers had partial truth through the ‘seed of the Logos’ and that whatever was rightly said by them belonged to Christians.
Called philosophy a gift of God and a ‘schoolmaster’ leading the Greeks to Christ (Stromata 1.5).
Built a philosophical theology in Platonic terms and taught philosophy to his students as preparation for Scripture.
Judged the Platonists closest to Christianity among the philosophers (City of God 8.5) while insisting they lacked the incarnation and humility of Christ.
influences/platonism-in-theology/critics: Asked ‘What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?’ (Prescription against Heretics 7) and called the philosophers the ‘patriarchs of the heretics’.
Argued in his History of Dogma (1886–90) that dogma was a Hellenisation of the simple Gospel, a thesis that shaped liberal Protestant historiography.
Anathemas associated with the council condemned Origenist doctrines such as the pre-existence of souls, marking a limit to Platonic speculation.
influences/platonism-in-theology/keptBy/: Eastern Orthodox and Catholic theology, which treat the patristic synthesis as normative
Anglican and Reformed patristic scholarship, which read the Fathers as faithful users of philosophy
Modern ‘Christian Platonist’ theologians such as David Bentley Hart
influences/platonism-in-theology/rejecte: Liberal Protestant historians in Harnack’s tradition, who sought a ‘de-Hellenised’ Gospel
Biblical theologians of the mid-twentieth century who contrasted Hebrew and Greek thought
Restorationist and Adventist groups that reject the immortal soul as a Platonic intrusion
influences/mystery-religions-debate/name: Mystery religions and the sacraments debate
influences/mystery-religions-debate/sour: Initiatory cults of the Graeco-Roman world — Eleusis, Isis, Dionysus, Cybele and Attis, Mithras — with secret rites, purifications and sacred meals
influences/mystery-religions-debate/chri: Mystery vocabulary for baptism and the eucharist (mysterion, initiation, illumination, sacramentum), the ‘discipline of the secret’ and mystagogical catechesis
influences/mystery-religions-debate/evid: Fourth-century borrowing of mystery language and ritual drama is well documented; the earlier claim that baptism and the eucharist themselves derive from the mysteries is rejected by most specialists, who point to Jewish origins and late or ambiguous pagan evidence.
influences/mystery-religions-debate/popu: Christian baptism and the Lord’s Supper were copied from pagan mystery religions, and Paul turned a Jewish teacher into a dying and rising saviour-god like Attis, Adonis or Osiris.
influences/mystery-religions-debate/what: The History of Religions School (Reitzenstein, Bousset) and Frazer’s The Golden Bough (1890–1915) popularised this view a century ago. Later scholarship — Arthur Darby Nock, Günter Wagner, A. J. M. Wedderburn, Walter Burkert and Jonathan Z. Smith — found that most supposed parallels rest on evidence later than the New Testament, on Christian sources, or on loose generalisation; the category of ‘dying and rising gods’ has been heavily criticised, though Tryggve Mettinger argued some Near Eastern examples existed while finding no evidence they shaped belief in Jesus. Baptism grew from Jewish ritual washing and John the Baptist; the eucharist from Jewish meal blessings, Passover and the Last Supper, attested by Paul c. 54 (1 Corinthians 11:23–26). After Constantine, however, the church deliberately used mystery language and ritual drama for initiation.
influences/mystery-religions-debate/summ: The resemblances between Christian sacraments and pagan mysteries were noticed in antiquity and became a major scholarly theory c. 1900. Today most historians see Jewish origins for the rites themselves, with real but later borrowing of mystery-cult vocabulary and atmosphere in the fourth century.
influences/mystery-religions-debate/stor:
The mystery cults were optional, initiatory forms of devotion within Graeco-Roman religion rather than separate religions. Initiates at Eleusis near Athens, or into the cults of Isis, Dionysus, Cybele and Attis, or Mithras, underwent purifications, fasting, secret revelations and sometimes sacred meals, and were promised a better lot in this life and the next. Their rites were secret, so our knowledge is fragmentary, much of it coming from later sources, including hostile Christian writers such as Clement of Alexandria and Firmicus Maternus (On the Error of Profane Religions, c. 346).

Christians noticed similarities early. Justin Martyr (1 Apology 66, c. 155) says that in the Mithraic rites bread and a cup of water are offered with certain formulas, an imitation, he argues, inspired by demons. Tertullian (On Baptism 5; Prescription 40) notes that initiates of Isis and Mithras were washed and that Mithras ‘signs his soldiers on the forehead’. Such writers did not deny the parallels; they explained them as diabolical counterfeits, which also shows that they were conscious of the risk of confusion.

Around 1900 the German History of Religions School, Richard Reitzenstein and Wilhelm Bousset, argued that Hellenistic Christianity, and Paul in particular, reshaped the faith on the model of the mysteries, and James Frazer collected ‘dying and rising gods’. Critics answered that the evidence is mostly later than Paul; that the taurobolium, a bull sacrifice once read as a ‘baptism in blood’ that gave rebirth, is attested in that form only in the fourth century, with the phrase ‘reborn for eternity’ appearing in an inscription of 376, possibly itself influenced by Christianity; and that Attis or Osiris do not rise in any sense comparable to the Gospel accounts. Jonathan Z. Smith’s Drudgery Divine (1990) also showed how Protestant polemic against Catholic ‘pagano-papism’ had coloured the comparison.

What is clearly documented is a fourth-century turn. As crowds sought baptism after Constantine, bishops presented initiation as an awe-inspiring mystery. The ‘discipline of the secret’ withheld the rites from the unbaptised; the newly baptised received ‘mystagogical’ instruction after Easter, as in the catecheses attributed to Cyril of Jerusalem and the sermons of Ambrose (On the Mysteries), John Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia. Words such as mysterion (Latin sacramentum, originally a soldier’s oath), photismos (illumination) and ‘initiation’ were used freely, and Clement had already called Christianity the true mysteries while mocking Eleusis (Exhortation 12).

The debate continues in popular culture and inter-church polemic. Some Protestant critics, such as Alexander Hislop in The Two Babylons (1853), accused Catholicism of perpetuating pagan mysteries, a work historians regard as unreliable. Catholics and Orthodox, for their part, speak of ‘the holy mysteries’ without embarrassment, seeing the shared vocabulary as a sign that Christ fulfils the longings expressed in pagan rites.
influences/mystery-religions-debate/howI: Baptism developed from Jewish purification rites and the baptism of John; the eucharist from Jewish meal practice and the Last Supper.
Apologists noticed pagan parallels and explained them as demonic imitations.
Greek-speaking Christians used the existing word mysterion, already present in Paul for God’s revealed plan, and Latin Christians used sacramentum.
After 313 bishops adopted secrecy, dramatic night-time rites and post-baptismal mystagogy to impress mass converts.
Modern comparative religion revived the comparison, and later scholarship critically tested it.
influences/mystery-religions-debate/exam: Justin Martyr on the Mithraic bread and cup (1 Apology 66).
Tertullian on washings in the cults of Isis and Mithras (On Baptism 5).
The Mystagogical Catecheses attributed to Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 350–390).
Ambrose’s On the Mysteries and On the Sacraments (c. 390) in Milan.
The taurobolium inscription of 376 (CIL VI 510) with ‘reborn for eternity’.
influences/mystery-religions-debate/defe: Invited pagans to the ‘truly sacred mysteries’ of the Logos in place of Eleusis (Exhortation to the Greeks 12).
Explained the rites of initiation to the newly baptised as awe-inspiring mysteries in his catechetical lectures.
Used the language of initiation and secrecy in his sermons On the Mysteries to the neophytes of Milan.
influences/mystery-religions-debate/crit: Treated the Mithraic meal as a demonic imitation of the eucharist.
Called pagan washings the devil’s mimicry of baptism.
Argued in The Two Babylons (1853) that Catholic sacraments continued Babylonian mysteries — a thesis historians reject as unfounded.
influences/mystery-religions-debate/kept: Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches, which call the sacraments ‘the holy mysteries’
Catholic liturgy, which restored mystagogy in the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults (1972)
influences/mystery-religions-debate/reje: Some Protestant and restorationist polemicists who see sacramental ritual as pagan
Christ-myth writers who argue Christianity was simply a mystery cult
